steps.what: Check you have what is needed: a Cloudflare account and about twenty minutes.
steps.why: The free plan works. Workers Paid ($5 a month) adds recomputing spreadsheets and signing in with a Claude subscription. No Claude account is needed to set up.

steps.what: Choose your group's short name, then install.
steps.why: It appears in addresses and signatures and can never change. A group that wants to stay unnamed picks one that reveals nothing.

steps.what: Let your copy test itself. Allow it to run the assistant's container if you are asked.
steps.why: The test proves your copy works before anyone relies on it.

steps.what: Claim your copy with the one-time password, then choose your own password.
steps.why: Only the person holding the one-time password can become the first administrator.

steps.what: Name the group, and add its logo if it has one.
steps.why: The group's name heads everything it publishes; Civicsmith is credited quietly at the foot.

steps.what: Verify the group's web address.
steps.why: Readers can then confirm that a published case really comes from your group.

steps.what: Choose the places whose rules apply, and the languages your members use.
steps.why: Deadlines, holidays and offices come from these places, never from Civicsmith itself.

steps.what: Review the offices, seats and holders Civicsmith filled in. Each is marked with where it came from.
steps.why: Requests go to offices by role, so correct anything before members rely on it.

steps.what: Read who in the group will see facts about people.
steps.why: Facts from public documents follow those documents; a project's own notes about a person stay inside the project.

steps.what: Decide whether to offer the assistant to your members.
steps.why: Each member who wants it connects their own Claude account. Nothing is shared, and everything works without it.

steps.what: Record who holds the hosting account.
steps.why: If you are ever unreachable, this is how the group gets back in.

steps.what: Invite your first members, and a second administrator now or later.
steps.why: With one administrator the group depends on one person. A second means it is never stuck.

steps.what: Optional: say who your group is. You will come back here when you finish or stop.
steps.why: It shapes how each member is welcomed. It locks nothing and is never required.

scripts.name: Welcome a new member
scripts.note: Final words once the redesign has settled (DEC-91).

steps.what: Choose your language.
steps.why: Everything that follows should be in words you read easily. It starts from your device's setting.

steps.what: Choose a handle and a password.
steps.why: The record shows your handle on your work. It needn't be your legal name: a known name lends credibility, a pen name shields you, and administrators still know who you are.

steps.what: This is your group's home: what it is working on, and what is waiting on you.
steps.why: Come back here whenever you lose your place.

steps.what: Two things to know first: a question's strength against its project's bar, and "Undetermined".
steps.why: You will see these everywhere. Every other mark is explained where you meet it, one tap away.

steps.what: Optional: connect your own Claude account, or skip.
steps.why: The assistant serves only you, and every journey works without it.

steps.what: Optional: tell the group about your own ties.
steps.why: Only you and the administrators see them, and they let a case disclose a tie honestly.

steps.what: Take a first step: join a project, capture a document, or record what you saw.
steps.why: One small act is enough to begin. Nothing here has to be done in order.

steps.what: Check what you are publishing: the case, its edition and its scope.
steps.why: Publishing is permanent. This is the last look before it.

steps.what: Check each finding's strength against the bar, and anything still open.
steps.why: A reader sees each finding's strengths. Anything still open is disclosed, never hidden.

steps.what: Read what the case leaves out, and who acknowledged it.
steps.why: Saying what a case does not cover is part of its honesty.

steps.what: Check each person the case names, with the reason they matter to a finding.
steps.why: A case cannot be signed while any reason is missing.

steps.what: Read what will be disclosed: the timeline as it stands, and any calculation that differs or is not tied to the record.
steps.why: Readers must see what the case could not settle.

steps.what: Read the group's declared bias as it will appear.
steps.why: Every published case carries the lens it was made through.

steps.what: Preview the public page as a stranger will see it.
steps.why: This is how a reader with no account meets your work.

steps.what: Each member publishing confirms they have no undeclared tie to anyone the case concerns.
steps.why: Including anyone paid in its money. A tie disclosed is a strength; one found later is not.

steps.what: Sign with your key.
steps.why: Publishing is permanent. Corrections come as a new edition, never by changing this one.

steps.what: Look first: is the record already public? Search what your group holds and where the office publishes.
steps.why: Much is public already. A copy from the office's own site holds up better than one found elsewhere.

steps.what: If you find it, capture it from its address. Then you are done.
steps.why: Capturing keeps a fingerprinted copy that cannot change under you.

steps.what: If not, choose the office that holds the records.
steps.why: The request goes to the office by its role, so it reaches whoever holds the post that day. You will see who that is.

steps.what: Say plainly what records you want.
steps.why: A clear description is harder to refuse, or to answer only in part.

steps.what: Choose the law the request goes under, from your group's places.
steps.why: The law sets the office's deadline. Where a faster kind of request fits, it is offered.

steps.what: Read the draft request and edit it until it is yours.
steps.why: The wizard only drafts. The words that are sent are yours.

steps.what: Approve the text.
steps.why: Approving is kept apart from sending, so you can stop between them.

steps.what: Send it the way the office accepts requests, then record that you sent it.
steps.why: Sending tells the office what your group is looking at. Recording the send starts the clock.

steps.what: Confirm the due date worked out from the law. Download it to your calendar if you like.
steps.why: You can see exactly how it was counted, and challenge it.

steps.what: Capture the claim where the city made it: a budget, a report to council, a press release.
steps.why: The claim itself is your first piece of evidence.

steps.what: Point at the words that make the claim.
steps.why: Every later step refers back to exactly what was said.

steps.what: Open the question: do the city's own records support the claim?
steps.why: A claim cannot be checked; a question can be answered, or shown undetermined.

steps.what: Pin down what the claim's words mean: what counts, and over what period. If the city never says, record that.
steps.why: A share means nothing until you know what was counted. A gap is recorded as undetermined, with its reason.

steps.what: Get the city's own records behind the claim: online, or by request.
steps.why: The claim should be checked against the city's own data, not anyone's impression.

steps.what: Work it out with the built-in calculation, or bind your own spreadsheet to the captured records.
steps.why: The method is shown with the result, so anyone can check it.

steps.what: Plan a spot-check: a recorded random draw picks which records members visit.
steps.why: A draw anyone can repeat means no one can say you picked the worst cases.

steps.what: Members visit and record what they find, with place, date and photo.
steps.why: Firsthand checks test whether the records match the street.

steps.what: Conclude with what the evidence supports, and say what would change it.
steps.why: A conclusion that names what would change it is one others can trust.

steps.what: What drew you in? A problem you live with, a person, a payment or contract, or something you read.
steps.why: Any of these is a good start. Civicsmith offers a first step from each.

steps.what: Say what you want to know, as a question.
steps.why: A question is something the record can answer: yes, no, or undetermined, and why.

steps.what: Find or capture a document that bears on it.
steps.why: Every answer rests on documents anyone could check.

steps.what: Point at the passage that matters.
steps.why: Citing a passage, not a whole document, shows exactly what you rely on.

steps.what: Say whether it supports the question or cuts against it.
steps.why: Evidence against is kept as carefully as evidence for.

steps.what: See the question's strength against the project's bar, and what would raise it.
steps.why: Strength is two grades, never one score: how well the documents are held and how firmly they are linked.

steps.what: What kind of group are you? Pick one or more, or describe your own.
steps.why: It shapes how each member is welcomed. It never limits what anyone can do.

steps.what: What do you focus on: issues, places, offices or agencies?
steps.why: New members see your focus first when they choose where to start.

steps.what: Why does the group exist? Say it in your own words.
steps.why: Your declared bias can start from what you write here.

steps.what: Who should see this: members only, or also your public page and the network directory?
steps.why: Members only is the default. A group that wants to stay unnamed keeps it that way.

steps.what: Who: their handle, and the cover the group knows them by. Not a legal name.
steps.why: The record never needs a legal name. Administrators keep the cover so they know who is who.

steps.what: What they may do. Contributing is the default.
steps.why: Give only what the person needs; you can change it later.

steps.what: Send the link yourself. It works once and expires after seven days.
steps.why: Civicsmith sends no email, so the link reaches them only through you.

steps.what: Or let people join through your website: create a website key, or turn on the reusable join link.
steps.why: Anyone let through can see the group's shared work, so each comes with limits and a daily cap.

steps.what: The assistant is optional, and serves only you.
steps.why: It runs on your own Claude account, never the group's. Everything works without it.

steps.what: Read what connecting means.
steps.why: Your questions, and what is read to answer them, go to Anthropic under your own account.

steps.what: Connect with your own Claude API key or your own subscription token. Or skip.
steps.why: Either serves only you. Skipping is a real choice: every journey stays open.

steps.what: For a subscription token: on your own computer, open a terminal, run claude setup-token, sign in, and paste what it prints here.
steps.why: The token is made by Anthropic's own sign-in on your computer. Civicsmith never sees your password.

steps.what: Set your daily limit.
steps.why: It caps what the assistant can spend on your account each day. An administrator may set a lower one for the copy.

steps.what: Choose whether the assistant may suggest things without being asked. It is off unless you turn it on.
steps.why: Some members want suggestions; others want quiet.

steps.what: You can disconnect at any time, here.
steps.why: Disconnecting removes the key or token from your group's copy.

steps.what: List your employer, relatives, and businesses you have an interest in.
steps.why: A case concerning any of them can then disclose the tie honestly.

steps.what: Only you and the administrators can see this.
steps.why: Your ties never appear in a case unless one concerns it, and then only as you choose.

steps.what: For each tie, choose how it is disclosed when a case concerns it: under your handle, or as the group.
steps.why: Disclosing as the group protects you while keeping the case honest.

steps.what: Capture a filing, or the court's register page.
steps.why: The proceeding is registered from what it says about itself.

steps.what: Register the proceeding from its caption: the court, the number, and a neutral label.
steps.why: A neutral label keeps your own view out of the record's name for it.

steps.what: Add the parties by role.
steps.why: Roles say who is suing, who is sued, and who is deciding.

steps.what: Follow its register: on a schedule, or by your own capture where the register needs a login.
steps.why: New filings are flagged, so nothing arrives unseen.

steps.what: Hold each order's requirements as obligations, with their reply dates.
steps.why: An order is a standard the office must meet. Its dates go into your queue.

steps.what: Capture the budget, financial report or contract.
steps.why: Every figure must point back to where it was printed.

steps.what: Read just the figures you need, each with its stage and period.
steps.why: Proposed, adopted, committed and paid are different facts. Mixing them is how money stories go wrong.

steps.what: Start a money trail.
steps.why: A trail gathers the figures one question needs.

steps.what: Include or leave out each item, with a reason.
steps.why: Your reasons show a reader why the trail adds up the way it does.

steps.what: Compare two sources of one figure, or what was committed against what was paid.
steps.why: Differences in basis, period or rounding are named, not hidden.

steps.what: Record an event from a cited passage: what, when, and how precisely you know the date.
steps.why: Every event points at its source. A date you only know roughly is recorded as rough.

steps.what: Add who took part and in what role: decided, signed, voted.
steps.why: Roles are what make an event useful to a finding.

steps.what: Link events: made under, answered, amended.
steps.why: Links let a reader follow one thread through the record.

steps.what: Keep a suspected cause as a hunch, never as a fact.
steps.why: A hunch is marked as yours and is never evidence.

steps.what: Review the two lanes before the case is signed: what they did, and what we did.
steps.why: The timeline is frozen into the case when it is signed.

steps.what: Choose how often to check, and until when.
steps.why: An end date is required, so no question runs forever.

steps.what: The search runs on schedule. With the assistant connected, it reads only what is new, on your account and within your limit.
steps.why: Without the assistant, new matches arrive as a list for you to read.

steps.what: The answer reaches your queue once.
steps.why: Only you see it; it is never shared.

steps.what: Stop it any time.
steps.why: Stopping is immediate, and nothing further is checked.

steps.what: Import the case into its own read-only project.
steps.why: Another group's work stays marked as theirs, and cannot be edited.

steps.what: Civicsmith recreates each finding and calculation from the case file. Watch each one's mark.
steps.why: Recreated, recreated in part, or did not recreate: you never rely on what you could not check.

steps.what: Accept what recreated, with a reason.
steps.why: Accepting names one edition and changes no grade.

steps.what: Watch the publisher's docket for new editions and corrections.
steps.why: Anything relying on the case is told when it changes.

steps.what: Choose the language.
steps.why: Civicsmith's own translations come with releases. Your group fills gaps and improves wording.

steps.what: See the words still untranslated.
steps.why: A missing word shows in English, never blank.

steps.what: With your own Claude account connected, ask the assistant to draft them. Each is marked "Draft".
steps.why: Without the assistant, type them yourself.

steps.what: Check and adopt each one.
steps.why: A word becomes the group's only when someone who knows the language adopts it.

steps.what: Choose the option, and say when to be reminded.
steps.why: Choosing records why this option, now.

steps.what: See what starting does, and anything that would stop it.
steps.why: Refusals are shown before anything runs.

steps.what: Start the action, addressed to the office by role.
steps.why: The office's holder that day is shown, so you know who will read it.

steps.what: Prepare what is sent. A template or draft is labelled until you make it yours.
steps.why: The words that leave the group are always a member's.

steps.what: Approve the text.
steps.why: Approving is kept apart from sending, so you can stop between them.

steps.what: Send it, then record that you sent it.
steps.why: This tells the office what your group is looking at, and starts the clock.

steps.what: The due date and next checkpoint go into your queue. A next step can wait on the reply.
steps.why: If no reply comes, the next step is ready without anyone remembering.
